Preoccupation

pree-ahk-yoo-PAY-shuhn -- from Latin prae- ('before') + occupare ('to seize, take possession of'). · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Preoccupation is a state of being absorbed in thought.

His preoccupation with the weather forecast meant he checked his phone every ten minutes before the wedding.

Worked Example

A student stares blankly at the exam question in front of her, unable to focus, because her mind keeps drifting back to a fight with her best friend that morning.

That inability to think about anything else, because one worry keeps seizing all of your attention beforehand, is exactly what a preoccupation is.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

absorption: the state of being fully engaged mentally in something

fixation: an unhealthy or excessive focus on something

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

indifference: a lack of interest or concern

detachment: emotional distance or lack of involvement

Where it sits · how tightly the mind is gripped — absorption → preoccupation → fixation

absorption vs. preoccupation: Absorption is more neutral than preoccupation -- being absorbed in a good book is a pleasant state, while preoccupation more often implies worry or distraction pulling your attention away from what's in front of you.

fixation vs. preoccupation: Fixation is stronger and more extreme than preoccupation -- a fixation is an excessive, hard-to-break focus that borders on unhealthy, while a preoccupation can be temporary and understandable, like worrying before a big test.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — pre-

prefix — pre-: before (Latin)

root — -occup-

root — -occup-: to seize, take hold of (Latin (occupare))

suffix — -ation

suffix — -ation: the act or result of; forms a noun (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin prae- ('before') plus occupare ('to seize') plus the noun suffix -ation: 'the state of being seized beforehand.' A preoccupation grabs hold of your mind before anything else can get its turn.

Use the root in a new word: occupy

Use the root in a new word: occupy: Protesters occupied the town square for three days before the council agreed to meet with them.

Word Choice

Preoccupation describes a mental state -- being so absorbed in one worry or interest that other things get ignored. The adjective form is 'preoccupied,' as in 'she seemed preoccupied all evening.'
